name: neon-ntt (hand-written Armv8-A Neon assembly NTTs for Dilithium, Kyber and Saber)
baseline: Dilithium reference C implementation (pq-crystals ref code compiled with gcc 10.3.0 -O3 on Cortex-A72 and Apple clang 12.0.5 -O3 on Apple M1); for Kyber and Saber the baseline is the previous Neon implementation by Nguyen and Gaj (re-benchmarked in SUPERCOP)
workload: Median or mean cycle counts for NTT, inverse NTT, base multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, inner product and full key generation, encapsulation/signing and decapsulation/verification of Dilithium2/3/5, Kyber512/768/1024 and Saber on a Raspberry Pi 4 (Cortex-A72) and an Apple M1.
claimed_speedup: Paper Table 4 (dilithium3, Cortex-A72): NTT 2 241 cycles vs 9 302 for the reference code (4.15x, derived from page data), inverse NTT 2 821 vs 11 633 (4.12x, derived); Apple M1 NTT 479 vs 2 865 (5.98x, derived). Table 5: dilithium2 MatrixVectorMul 26 268 vs 135 182 cycles on Cortex-A72 (5.15x, derived) and 5 316 vs 45 742 on M1 (8.6x, derived). Table 6 (dilithium3, Cortex-A72): key generation 515 776 vs 743 166 cycles (1.44x, derived), signing 1 089 387 vs 2 308 598 (2.12x, derived), verification 447 460 vs 728 866 (1.63x, derived). Against prior Neon work the paper states kyber768 MatrixVectorMul is 1.7x faster on Cortex-A72 and 2.1x on M1, full Kyber 9-14% faster on Cortex-A72 and 26-41% on M1, Saber MatrixVectorMul 2.0x on Cortex-A72.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 10.3.0 -O3 on Cortex-A72 (full schemes through SUPERCOP 20210604); Apple clang 12.0.5 -O3 on Apple M1
hardware: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B (Broadcom BCM2711, Arm Cortex-A72 at 1.5 GHz); Apple M1 Mac mini
stars_or_usage: 34 stars; artifact of a TCHES 2022 paper
tradeoffs: Armv8-A (aarch64) only, tuned for Cortex-A72 and Apple M1. The benchmark harness is only tested on Cortex-A72; user-mode cycle-counter access needs a kernel module there and root on the M1. The speedups combine new algorithms (Barrett multiplication, asymmetric multiplication, interleaved butterflies) with hand-written assembly, so they are not a pure assembly-versus-compiler comparison. Bundled third-party code is CC0, Apache-2.0, MIT or public domain.
caveats: The Dilithium baseline is the unoptimised portable reference code, so the 4-8x kernel gains largely measure hand vectorisation against scalar C; the Kyber and Saber comparisons are against another Neon implementation (Nguyen-Gaj, intrinsics), where gains are roughly 1.1-2.1x. The paper notes the Nguyen-Gaj NTT cycle counts omit the final reduction. Cortex-A72 numbers are medians of 10 000 runs, Apple M1 numbers are averages. The repository was updated after publication; the README says to use commit a96c17dbe74ac7675c785a728396e216555c432b to reproduce the paper. Cycle counts were read from the paper PDF (copy on the author's github.io repository), not re-run. The hand-written files are the __asm_NTT.S, __asm_iNTT.S, __asm_base_mul.S and __asm_poly.S sources in each scheme's ntt directory (kyber768/ntt confirmed).
found_via: GitHub: neon-ntt/neon-ntt repo page, README and kyber768/ntt directory listing; paper PDF (ePrint 2021/986, TCHES 2022 issue 1) read from vincentvbh/vincentvbh.github.io/papers through raw.githubusercontent.com

name: crc32-vpmsum (POWER8 vpmsum CRC32 and CRC32C in hand-written assembly)
baseline: slice-by-8 table-driven CRC32C in C (slice_by_8_bench, built from the same Makefile with -O2); the README also cites the Linux kernel btrfs checksum path as a second baseline
workload: CRC32C (polynomial 0x11EDC6F41) over a 32 kB buffer, 5 000 000 iterations, L1-resident, timed with the shell time command; separate kernel test of btrfs writes to a ramdisk.
claimed_speedup: The vpmsum accelerated CRC is 'just over 41x faster' than slice-by-8: 2.937 seconds (crc32_bench) vs 122.220 seconds (slice_by_8_bench) for 5 000 000 x 32 kB. About 52 GiB/s or 13.6 bytes/cycle on a 4.1 GHz POWER8 (theoretical limit 16 bytes/cycle). The kernel btrfs write test is 3.8x faster.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile CFLAGS: -m64 -g -O2 -mcpu=power8 -mcrypto -mpower8-vector -maltivec -mvsx (assembly built with -m64 -g); gcc is implied by the README but no compiler version is stated
tradeoffs: POWER8 and later only (needs the vpmsum vector crypto instructions). Constants are generated by make for a chosen CRC polynomial (CRC32C or Ethernet CRC32 shown), so each polynomial needs its own constants header and renamed symbols. Two variants ship: pure assembly (crc32.S plus crc32_wrapper.c) and a gcc vector-intrinsics version (vec_crc32.c).
caveats: README numbers are undated and from one machine and one 32 kB L1-resident buffer, so they are best-case throughput. The baseline is a table method in C, not a library such as zlib, and POWER has no scalar CRC instruction to compare against. The README does not benchmark the C intrinsics version (vec_crc32_bench exists in the Makefile), so the share of the gain due to hand-written assembly rather than vpmsum itself is not shown. The btrfs 3.8x figure comes with no setup details.
found_via: WebSearch for hand-written POWER8 / ppc64le assembly versus C speedups (a libgcrypt vpmsum CRC patch snippet) led to the repo; README and Makefile opened through raw.githubusercontent.com and the repo commits page

name: seelabs/nasm (AVX2 hex encoder and decoder for 256-bit values in NASM)
baseline: reference C++ hex encode and decode routines taken from rippled (compiled with g++ -O3 according to build.sh)
workload: Encode a 32-byte binary value into 64 hex characters (encode_hex256) and decode 64 hex characters into 32 bytes (decode_hex256), 100 million iterations each, test driver src/main.cpp.
claimed_speedup: README table: encoder 1790 ms (C reference) vs 319 ms (assembly), 5.6x (derived from page data); decoder 4694 ms vs 561 ms, 8.4x (derived from page data). README prose says 'about 10x faster than the reference C++ implementation'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. build.sh uses nasm -felf64 and g++ -std=c++14 -O3; CMakeLists.txt instead defaults to clang with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug, so it is unclear which build produced the table.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1505M v6 at 3.00 GHz
tradeoffs: x86-64 with AVX2 only, Linux System V calling convention only, fixed 32-byte (64 hex digit) inputs. No LICENSE file in the repository root, so the code must not be copied. Author states it is for learning and not well tested.
caveats: The kernels are specialised to one fixed size while the baseline handles any length, so part of the gain comes from specialisation rather than assembly itself. The README states the 10x figure is not matched by its own table (5.6x and 8.4x). Only one machine, one run, no compiler version, and the build used for the table is ambiguous (build.sh -O3 versus CMake Debug default). The README also reports that an AVX base58 coefficient routine gave only about 6% overall, and its 10x base58 gain is plain C++, not assembly. A verifier could raise this to tier A if the -O3 build in build.sh is accepted as the documented build.
found_via: WebSearch 'hand-written assembly vs C reference benchmark ... NASM AVX2 README' surfaced the seelabs/nasm hex codec; repo page, readme.md, build.sh and CMakeLists.txt opened

name: Raspberry Pi Pico SDK hand-coded RP2040 float and memory routines (pico_float, pico_mem_ops)
baseline: the compiler's soft-float library (libgcc) and C library memcpy/memset on the Cortex-M0+ cores of the RP2040
workload: Single-precision floating point arithmetic and math functions, and memcpy/memset, on RP2040; the repository contains no benchmark for these.
claimed_speedup: No numbers. The pico_float header says the RP2040 'pico' implementations, hand coded in the bootrom and the SDK, 'are generally faster and smaller than those provided by the C compiler/library', though they do not support all features of a fully compliant floating point implementation. The pico_mem_ops header only says it provides 'optimized replacement implementations of the compiler built-in memcpy, memset and related functions'.
hardware: RP2040 (dual Arm Cortex-M0+); RP2350 variants use VFP or DCP hardware instead
stars_or_usage: 5.0k stars; the standard SDK for Raspberry Pi RP2040 and RP2350 boards
tradeoffs: RP2-series only. The RP2040 software float routines are not fully IEEE-compliant ('usually fine for the majority of cases'). On RP2350 the fastest option relies on the Arm FPU or the double-precision coprocessor rather than hand-written software routines.
caveats: Tier D: the only performance statement is qualitative. The cycle tables that back it are in the RP2040 datasheet, which this session could not reach (host blocked), so no number is recorded. Part of the RP2040 float code lives in the chip bootrom (the header says 'from the bootrom and the SDK'), not in this SDK alone.
found_via: GitHub: recalled while screening Cortex-M assembly libraries; opened the SDK's pico_float and pico_mem_ops headers through raw.githubusercontent.com and the repo page and commits page
